Appendix S1 MolRSI framework

S1.1 Resource library construction

Resource retrieval and synthesis. The Explore Agent generates task-specific queries about scientific methods, software and benchmark evaluation using the task description and available dataset information. It searches literature and web sources, removes duplicate results and ranks the remaining resources by relevance to the task. The retrieved material is summarized to identify models, methods, tools, benchmarks and associated implementations for skill construction.

Resource analysis and skill construction. The Explore Agent examines the retrieved resources and their available code, documentation and usage examples. It prioritizes resources for skill construction according to task relevance and the requested skill categories. When repository code is available, static analysis of Python abstract syntax trees recovers public interfaces and their arguments. These interfaces, together with model definitions and training or inference examples, inform the skill instructions. Additional searches supply supporting repositories or documentation when the initial material is incomplete.

Library organization and skill contents. A shared index lists each skill’s name, category and purpose. Each skill describes how to use the resource and links these instructions to available implementations, dependencies, usage examples and source references. Where relevant, it also specifies feature representations and whether computed features could be reused. The contents are summarized in Table S1.

Checks during construction. The Explore Agent checks package identity and examines Python usage examples for syntax and import-name inconsistencies. When an execution environment is available, it also checks dependency availability and selected interfaces. Detected problems prompt revisions to installation instructions, dependencies or usage examples. These checks precede execution validation when a skill is first used.

Execution validation and reuse. When a newly constructed skill is first used, MolRSI runs a usage example in an isolated environment. Execution errors guide repairs to the code, dependencies or environment settings. The example is rerun until it completes successfully or reaches the repair-attempt limit. Skills that pass are tagged as validated and retained in the resource library for reuse. Skills that remain unsuccessful are removed.

Incremental expansion. The Explore Agent could expand an existing resource library by retrieving additional resources and identifying skills not already present. Existing skills are retained. New skills undergo the same construction checks and first-use execution validation, and the shared index is updated to include them.

S1.2 Persistent memory

Workflow development generates experience about candidate performance, proposed modifications and execution. MolRSI retains this experience in solution, refinement and execution memory, together with the tasks and conditions under which it was obtained. These memories guide later search decisions within and across tasks (Figure S1).

Solution memory. For each evaluated workflow, solution memory stores the task description, task type, dataset and dataset size, together with the workflow’s executable code, configuration and execution status. The configuration specifies the workflow family, component models and methods, architecture, hyperparameters, data processing, training objective and training or generation procedure. Development scores are retained with their evaluation metric and, where applicable, data split and random seed. A workflow that failed before evaluation retains its failure status without receiving a development score. Scores from completed workflows provide evidence about which families performed well on related tasks and which individual workflows are suitable for further refinement or transfer. The historical score normalization, family selection and parent selection procedures are specified in Section S1.3.

Refinement memory. Refinement memory stores the original workflow, the revised workflow, the task and the proposed changes. Changes are described by the affected component and its settings, such as an architecture change, the use of parameter-efficient fine-tuning, a different loss function, altered data processing or a change in learning rate. The agent’s reason for proposing a change is retained alongside the result of testing it. When the original and revised workflows are evaluated under the same protocol, both development scores and their difference are stored. Improvements, declines, unchanged scores and execution failures are all retained. If a proposal changes several components, its outcome is associated with the combined modification. For a subsequent proposal, the agent retrieves relevant earlier changes and their outcomes, including previous attempts derived from the selected parent workflow.

Execution memory. Execution memory stores the execution history of workflows and the usable skills in the resource library. For each attempt, it retains the dataset and its size, hardware and software environment, execution status and available runtime measurements. Resource measurements include elapsed time, GPU time, processing speed and GPU memory use. Where measured, training time per sample per epoch relates runtime to dataset size and training duration. These measurements inform later resource allocation and timeout settings. For each failure, the memory retains the failed stage, error messages, execution logs and the cause when identified. It also stores each attempted repair, including changes to code, dependencies or environment settings, and whether re-execution succeeded. This experience guides repairs when similar errors recur.

Updates within and across tasks. Memory is updated after each execution attempt and used to guide subsequent iterations. Experience retained from completed tasks could also guide later searches or direct workflow transfer. When an evaluation used fixed source-task experience, each target began with the same experience, and updates from one target were not shared with other targets. Application-specific experience pools are described in Sections S3.2 and S4.1. Held-out test scores are excluded from memory updates and search decisions. Section S1.3 describes how the updated memory guides the search policy.

S1.3 Recursive self-improvement of the search policy

Search representation. MolRSI uses experience-guided Monte Carlo tree search over a forest of executable workflows. Initial workflows form the roots of separate trees, and each node represents a concrete workflow with its specification, execution status, development scores, resource use, logs and generated artifacts. A workflow selected for modification is the parent, and the revised workflow is its child. An edge represents the proposed changes, such as a different representation, architecture, objective, data-processing procedure or composition of methods. Workflows based on a common model or computational approach are grouped into families. The five steps below specify how current-task observations and historical experience guide search decisions.

Step 1: Selecting workflow families. Family selection combines the best available current-task development performance, an exploration bonus and a historical transfer score. Historical workflow scores are first standardized within each source task and then aggregated using task-similarity weights. The family-level score enters selection as an additive term. A corresponding workflow-level historical score enters parent sampling in Step 2 as a multiplicative factor. The normalization and aggregation used by both steps are defined together below.

Historical score normalization. Let xτ​(v)x_{\tau}(v) denote the development score of workflow vv on source task τ\tau, and let 𝒱τ\mathcal{V}_{\tau} contain completed workflows with finite development scores on that task. Scores are first oriented so that larger values indicate better performance:

sτ​(v)={xτ​(v),for a higher-is-better metric,−xτ​(v),for a lower-is-better metric.s_{\tau}(v)=\begin{cases}x_{\tau}(v),&\text{for a higher-is-better metric},\\[3.0pt] -x_{\tau}(v),&\text{for a lower-is-better metric}.\end{cases} (3)

Each score is then normalized relative to the other completed workflows on the same source task:

s~τ​(v)=sτ​(v)−medianu∈𝒱τ⁡sτ​(u)max⁡{MADu∈𝒱τ⁡(sτ​(u)),ϵ}.\widetilde{s}_{\tau}(v)=\frac{s_{\tau}(v)-\operatorname{median}_{u\in\mathcal{V}_{\tau}}s_{\tau}(u)}{\max\!\left\{\operatorname{MAD}_{u\in\mathcal{V}_{\tau}}(s_{\tau}(u)),\epsilon\right\}}. (4)

Here, MAD⁡(s)=median⁡|s−median⁡(s)|\operatorname{MAD}(s)=\operatorname{median}|s-\operatorname{median}(s)| is the median absolute deviation from the median, and ϵ>0\epsilon>0 prevents division by zero. The normalized score is mapped to a bounded utility:

s¯τ​(v)=2​σ​(s~τ​(v))−1,σ⁡(x)=11+e−x.\bar{s}_{\tau}(v)=2\sigma\!\left(\widetilde{s}_{\tau}(v)\right)-1,\qquad\sigma(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}. (5)

The resulting utility lies in [−1,1][-1,1], allowing historical outcomes measured on different scales to be aggregated without an unbounded contribution from a single task. All scores used in this calculation were available during development of the source workflow; held-out test scores are excluded.

Task-similarity weights. For a target task τ0\tau_{0}, the contribution of source task τ\tau is weighted according to evaluation-metric compatibility, task type, dataset size and task-description similarity:

w⁡(τ,τ0)=wmetric​(τ,τ0)​wtype​(τ,τ0)​wsize​(τ,τ0)​wemb​(τ,τ0).w(\tau,\tau_{0})=w_{\mathrm{metric}}(\tau,\tau_{0})\,w_{\mathrm{type}}(\tau,\tau_{0})\,w_{\mathrm{size}}(\tau,\tau_{0})\,w_{\mathrm{emb}}(\tau,\tau_{0}). (6)

The non-negative factors wmetricw_{\mathrm{metric}} and wtypew_{\mathrm{type}} encode compatibility of evaluation metrics and task types. Dataset-size similarity is calculated as

wsize​(τ,τ0)=exp⁡[−γ​|log⁡|𝒟τ|−log⁡|𝒟τ0||],w_{\mathrm{size}}(\tau,\tau_{0})=\exp\!\left[-\gamma\left|\log|\mathcal{D}_{\tau}|-\log|\mathcal{D}_{\tau_{0}}|\right|\right], (7)

where |𝒟τ||\mathcal{D}_{\tau}| denotes the dataset size associated with task τ\tau, and γ>0\gamma>0 controls the penalty for size differences. Description similarity is calculated from task-description embeddings 𝐞τ\mathbf{e}_{\tau} and 𝐞τ0\mathbf{e}_{\tau_{0}}:

wemb​(τ,τ0)=max⁡{cos⁡(𝐞τ,𝐞τ0),0}.w_{\mathrm{emb}}(\tau,\tau_{0})=\max\!\left\{\cos(\mathbf{e}_{\tau},\mathbf{e}_{\tau_{0}}),0\right\}. (8)

Family and workflow transfer scores. Let 𝒯f\mathcal{T}_{f} denote the eligible source tasks containing an evaluated workflow from family ff, and let 𝒱τ,f\mathcal{V}_{\tau,f} denote the evaluated workflows from that family on source task τ\tau. The family-level transfer score is

transfer⁡(f)=∑τ∈𝒯fw⁡(τ,τ0)​meanv∈𝒱τ,f​s¯τ​(v)∑τ∈𝒯fw⁡(τ,τ0).\operatorname{transfer}(f)=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}_{f}}w(\tau,\tau_{0})\,\operatorname{mean}_{v\in\mathcal{V}_{\tau,f}}\bar{s}_{\tau}(v)}{\displaystyle\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}_{f}}w(\tau,\tau_{0})}. (9)

This calculation first averages performance within each source task and then combines those task-level averages. For a target-task workflow viv_{i}, let 𝒯i\mathcal{T}_{i} denote source tasks containing an eligible historical match. The matching rule uses workflow family and modification type, and matched⁡(vi,τ)\operatorname{matched}(v_{i},\tau) denotes the historical workflow identified on source task τ\tau. The workflow-level transfer score is

transfer⁡(vi)=∑τ∈𝒯iw⁡(τ,τ0)​s¯τ​(matched⁡(vi,τ))∑τ∈𝒯iw⁡(τ,τ0).\operatorname{transfer}(v_{i})=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}_{i}}w(\tau,\tau_{0})\,\bar{s}_{\tau}\!\left(\operatorname{matched}(v_{i},\tau)\right)}{\displaystyle\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}_{i}}w(\tau,\tau_{0})}. (10)

Tasks without an eligible record are excluded from the corresponding numerator and denominator. These weighted averages are defined when the total task weight is positive. With non-negative task weights and utilities in [−1,1][-1,1], each defined transfer score also lies in [−1,1][-1,1].

Family-selection rule. Let bb index family-selection decisions, ℱeligible\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{eligible}} denote the eligible workflow families and nb​(f)≥1n_{b}(f)\geq 1 denote the visit count for family ff. The next family is selected according to

fb=arg​maxf∈ℱeligible⁡[exploitb⁡(f)⏟current-taskperformance+α​ln⁡(b+1)nb​(f)⏟explorationbonus+transfer⁡(f)⏟historicaltransfer].f_{b}=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{f\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{eligible}}}\Biggl[\underbrace{\operatorname{exploit}_{b}(f)}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{current-task}\\ \text{performance}\end{subarray}}+\underbrace{\alpha\sqrt{\frac{\ln(b+1)}{n_{b}(f)}}}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{exploration}\\ \text{bonus}\end{subarray}}+\underbrace{\operatorname{transfer}(f)}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{historical}\\ \text{transfer}\end{subarray}}\Biggr]. (11)

The exploitation term summarizes the best current-task development performance within family ff, including stability and overfitting adjustments, on a scale from zero to one. The coefficient α\alpha controls exploration, with larger bonuses for less-visited families [? ]. Historical evidence enters through the family-level transfer score defined above. Historical experience guides initial exploration, and current-task scores are incorporated as evaluations become available.

Step 2: Selecting parent workflows. Let 𝒱\mathcal{V} contain completed, non-ensemble workflows with finite development scores on the current task. For workflow vi∈𝒱v_{i}\in\mathcal{V}, let qiq_{i} denote the current-task score supplied to the sampler and cic_{i} the number of existing children. Sampling weights and probabilities are

wi\displaystyle w_{i} =σ⁡(β​qi−medianvj∈𝒱⁡qjmax⁡{MADvj∈𝒱⁡(qj),ϵ})​11+ci​[1+λ​transfer⁡(vi)],\displaystyle=\sigma\!\left(\beta\frac{q_{i}-\operatorname{median}_{v_{j}\in\mathcal{V}}q_{j}}{\max\!\left\{\operatorname{MAD}_{v_{j}\in\mathcal{V}}(q_{j}),\epsilon\right\}}\right)\frac{1}{1+c_{i}}\left[1+\lambda\,\operatorname{transfer}(v_{i})\right], (12)
p⁡(vi)\displaystyle p(v_{i}) =wi∑vj∈𝒱wj.\displaystyle=\frac{w_{i}}{\displaystyle\sum_{v_{j}\in\mathcal{V}}w_{j}}.

The coefficient β\beta controls sensitivity to standardized current-task scores. The factor 1/(1+ci)1/(1+c_{i}) reduces repeated expansion of the same parent, and λ\lambda controls the contribution of historical transfer. The normalized sampler requires non-negative weights and a positive total weight.

Step 3: Proposing workflow modifications. The agent retrieves previous modifications, their rationales and their outcomes from refinement memory to guide changes to the selected parent workflow. Each proposal specifies the changes and their rationale. The proposed workflow is checked for the required format, duplication of an existing candidate and feasibility of execution. Malformed, duplicate or infeasible proposals do not become completed workflow nodes. The proposed modification and its observed outcome are added to refinement memory after execution, including changes that reduced performance or failed to execute.

Step 4: Executing and evaluating workflows. The proposed child workflow is implemented and run in an isolated environment using the task-specific evaluation procedure. Execution memory informs environment settings and resource allocation. If setup or execution fails, the agent first searches execution memory for similar errors and successful repairs. Relevant experience guides changes to the code, dependencies or environment settings. If no suitable repair is available or the problem persists, the agent diagnoses the current failure and proposes further changes. The workflow is rerun after each repair, within the repair-attempt limit and computational budget. Successful evaluations supply development scores; all attempts retain their execution status, logs, resource measurements and repair outcomes. Failed evaluations count toward the workflow-evaluation allowance, but repairs of the same candidate do not consume additional evaluations.

Step 5: Updating search policy to guide subsequent searches. After each attempt, MolRSI adds the workflow and its development score or failure status to solution memory. It stores the proposed modification and its outcome in refinement memory, and runtime, resource use, errors and repair outcomes in execution memory. The corresponding node and edge in the search forest are also updated. The updated memories guide subsequent family selection, parent sampling, modification proposals and execution. These updates change the effective search policy πt\pi_{t}, whose subsequent evaluations generate experience for the next memory update. This feedback implements the RSI loop expressed by MtM_{t}, EtE_{t} and πt\pi_{t} in Equation 1.

Historical and current task updates. Current task executions update development scores, visit counts and the experience used for subsequent refinement and execution. When the source memory was fixed for an evaluation, its historical transfer scores remained unchanged during that target-task search. Under continued use across tasks, experience from newly completed tasks could contribute to transfer estimates for later searches. The bounded transfer scores serve as empirical selection priors; their boundedness alone does not establish a standard target-task or node-level regret guarantee.

Search termination and returned workflow. Search stops when the task-specific limit on evaluation attempts or computation time is reached. MolRSI returns the successfully evaluated workflow with the best current-task development score. This is the best evaluated workflow under the stated criterion and budget, rather than a global optimum. The evaluation unit and accounting for failed attempts and repairs are specified in Supplementary Information S2.

Workflow transfer with and without further search. MolRSI could use experience from previous tasks to retrieve a workflow for direct transfer or initialize a new search. It first identifies the best matching previously completed task using task type, evaluation metric, dataset size and task description similarity. It then retrieves that source task’s workflow with the best development score from solution memory. This source task routing is distinct from the family- and workflow-level transfer scores used in Steps 1 and 2. In zero-search mode, the retrieved configuration is applied to the new task without proposing or comparing alternative workflows. Model parameters are fitted using the new task’s training data where required, and fitting and execution still incur computational cost. Alternatively, the retrieved workflow becomes a starting point for Steps 1–5 under the new task’s limits on evaluation attempts and computation time.

Appendix S2 Comparison with baseline agents

S2.1 Shared evaluation protocol

Agents and comparison settings. We compared MolRSI with Biomni [? ], Claude Science [? ], STELLA [? ] and Codex [? ] on antibacterial prediction and protein binder ranking workflow development. The antibacterial benchmark additionally included Claude Code [? ]. Within each benchmark, agents received the same task inputs, permitted development data, evaluation objective and workflow-evaluation allowance. Each agent used its native tools and workflow development procedures without a common predefined workflow search space. The task-specific instructions and permitted tools are described below.

Task instructions and permitted tools. For baseline searches in antibacterial prediction and protein ranking, prompts specified the task inputs, fixed data partitions, development objective and metric, evaluation allowance, required outputs and permitted tools. No starting prediction model or ranking workflow was prescribed. The instructions prohibited changes to the fixed data, partitions, and data-loading or evaluation code, hidden candidate evaluations, and the use of held-out labels or performance for workflow development or selection. Independent baseline runs also prohibited reuse of results, code or model choices from another baseline run.

Search permissions and execution records. These baseline agents could search using their native capabilities, and local agents could install software packages. Search, installation, environment inspection and deterministic feature caching independent of the labels did not consume candidate evaluations. Candidates were evaluated sequentially, with subsequent choices based on the preceding development results. Each candidate’s code, outputs, execution status, logs, runtime, development scores and held-out test predictions were retained.

Evaluation allowance and repair. A candidate counted as one workflow evaluation once its evaluation began, including evaluations that failed or timed out. Repair attempts for the same candidate did not count as additional workflow evaluations. The authors supplied the task inputs and evaluation interfaces without selecting workflow components, repairing candidates or granting additional retries during the runs.

LLM backbones. MolRSI used Claude Sonnet 5 throughout the antibacterial and protein studies. In the antibacterial prediction and protein ranking benchmarks, the baseline agents also used Claude Sonnet 5, except Codex, which used GPT-5.5. Claude Science used Claude Opus 5 for prospective binder design.

API access and agent interfaces. MolRSI accessed its model through the Anthropic API. Biomni ran on its own platform and used its platform-provided environment for workflow planning and execution. Its outputs were not independently reproduced outside that platform. Claude Science used its scientific workflow-development interface. STELLA ran in self-evolve mode using the implementation available at https://github.com/asfarasimconcerned/STELLA. Codex and Claude Code [? ] used their native coding-agent interfaces, with writable workflow directories and fixed data and evaluation helpers.

Computational resources. Across antibacterial prediction, protein ranking and prospective binder design, the authors provided GPUs to agent baselines, and each agent controlled job scheduling and GPU use within its task-specific budget. Their prompts imposed no hard wall-clock limit. These hardware assignments describe the four local baselines and do not specify the resources provided by the Biomni platform.

S2.2 Antibacterial task instructions and permitted tools

Task inputs and evaluation. We evaluated MolRSI with and without RSI alongside the baseline agents on the six antibacterial target tasks. Systems received the same molecular inputs, fixed partitions, development objective and allowance of 20 attempted workflow evaluations per task. A completed candidate evaluation covered all five fixed splits in Section S3.1, rather than counting each split as a separate attempt. Mean validation AUPRC guided search and final workflow selection; test predictions were scored after search.

Search permissions and execution records. Antibacterial baselines followed the shared search permissions and execution-record requirements in Section S2.1, using validation scores as their development feedback.

Computational resources. Claude Code, Claude Science, STELLA and Codex were each assigned one NVIDIA L40S GPU and 20 CPU threads. Scheduling followed the shared protocol in Section S2.1.

Complete task prompt and substitutions. The Claude Code prompt for the E. coli task is reproduced below, with machine-specific paths anonymized and device indices omitted. Path prefixes are represented by <BASELINE_ROOT>; the remaining instructions are unchanged. Biomni received the same task instructions through its native interface. Dataset names, identifiers, split sizes and loading checks were adjusted for each task (Table S2).

TASK DESCRIPTION
——
# Molecular Property Prediction Benchmark — activity_E_coli
## Task
Predict the molecular property endpoint **activity_E_coli** from molecular SMILES strings.
- Dataset id: ‘antibiotic__activity_E_coli‘
- Dataset family: antibiotic
- Category: activity
- Task type: classification
- Primary metric: **AUPRC** (higher is better)
- Train/validation pool: 35340-35341 molecules depending on seed
- Held-out test set: 3926-3927 molecules depending on seed; you must produce per-seed test predictions for every candidate
- Split: {"fingerprint": {"nbits": 2048, "radius": 2, "type": "Morgan"}, "method": "greedy_leader_tanimoto", "similarity_threshold": 0.4, "stratified_by": "Y", "test_fraction": 0.1, "val_fraction": 0.1}
## Data
The uploaded ‘dataset_activity_E_coli/‘ directory belongs only to **activity_E_coli**. It contains ‘meta.json‘ and five fixed split directories, ‘seed_1/‘ through ‘seed_5/‘. Before running any experiment, verify that ‘dataset_activity_E_coli/meta.json‘ has ‘name‘ equal to ‘activity_E_coli‘, ‘dataset_id‘ equal to ‘antibiotic__activity_E_coli‘, and primary metric equal to ‘AUPRC‘; stop and report a dataset mismatch if any value differs. Each seed directory contains ‘train.csv‘, ‘val.csv‘, and ‘test.csv‘. The labeled training and validation files contain ‘Drug_ID‘, ‘Drug‘ (SMILES), ‘Y‘ (label/target), and may contain precomputed molecule-derived descriptor columns. The test files contain the same columns, including ‘Y‘; ‘Y‘ is present only so that predictions can be aligned and scored afterwards, and must never be read during training, tuning, or model selection.
Use the fixed split files directly:
“‘python
import pandas as pd
SEEDS = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
for seed in SEEDS:
train_df = pd.read_csv(f"dataset_activity_E_coli/seed_{seed}/train.csv")
val_df = pd.read_csv(f"dataset_activity_E_coli/seed_{seed}/val.csv")
“‘
Model selection is validation-only: never let test labels or test performance influence training, tuning, search, or candidate choice. For every candidate you evaluate, do generate and save per-seed test predictions via ‘prepare.save_predictions‘ — they are scored afterwards, outside this run. Do not create alternative train/validation splits and do not merge train and validation during search.
## Evaluation
The primary validation metric is **AUPRC** (higher is better). Evaluate each candidate independently on all five fixed seed splits. Compute the metric separately for each seed, then report the arithmetic mean and sample standard deviation (‘ddof=1‘) across the five values. Use ‘roc_auc_score‘ for AUROC, ‘average_precision_score‘ for AUPRC, ‘mean_absolute_error‘ for MAE, and ‘spearmanr(…).statistic‘ for Spearman. Classification metrics must be computed from positive-class probabilities, not hard class labels.
For every candidate, print exactly one validation line for each seed followed by the aggregate result:

All five seed lines and the final result line are mandatory. The five-seed validation mean is the sole optimization and model-selection target.
## Experiment Budget
Run exactly 20 complete candidate experiments, named ‘step_01‘ through ‘step_20‘. One budget unit is one candidate method trained and evaluated on all five fixed seed splits. Evaluate one candidate at a time. A candidate whose evaluation starts but crashes or times out still consumes its numbered step. Environment inspection and deterministic label-independent feature caching do not consume a step, but unlogged pilot experiments, hidden parameter sweeps, and extra candidate evaluations are not allowed.

Preserve every step’s artifacts without overwriting earlier steps. After ‘step_20‘, select the completed candidate with the best five-seed validation mean according to the stated metric direction and preserve its source code as the final solution.

At the end, report the selected step, its five per-seed validation values, validation mean +/- sample standard deviation, the number of completed steps out of 20, failed steps, and the paths to the selected source code and complete step logs.

S2.3 Protein task instructions and permitted tools

Task inputs and evaluation.

Ranking workflow search. Claude Science, Biomni, STELLA and Codex received target structures, candidate collections, permitted development labels and a task-specific ranking objective. Each baseline was asked to return a workflow assigning a scalar score to each target–binder complex. AUPRC on the 13 search targets guided workflow selection for each miniprotein-binder task. AUROC on the two gp100 collections guided selection for the pMHC task. Selected workflows were fixed before held-out evaluation using the partitions in Section S4.1.

Prospective design workflow. The recorded Claude Science protocol used an independent session per target. The recorded instructions supplied HLA heavy-chain and β2\beta_{2}-microglobulin sequences and MSAs, on- and off-target peptide sequences, an 80–120-residue binder range, epitope hints and novelty references. Target coordinates were not supplied. The requested output was 500 ranked designs, using the prescribed on- and off-target scoring criterion and diversity constraints described in Section S4.5.

Search permissions and execution records.

Ranking workflow search. All four protein ranking baselines followed the same search permissions and execution-record requirements as the antibacterial baselines (Section S2.1), using scores on the permitted search targets as their development feedback.

Prospective design workflow. Claude Science accessed and installed tools under its own platform rules. It chose generator settings, additional sampling and refinement steps within the task’s sampling, scoring and diversity requirements. Following Anthropic’s published prompt (source below), the agent was asked to save design sequences and structures, records of how each design was generated and refined, scores, run configurations and logs. Failed checks and runs were also to be recorded (Section S4.5).

Computational resources. Both ranking and prospective design followed the shared scheduling and wall-clock policy in Section S2.1.

Ranking workflow search. Claude Science, STELLA and Codex each received 300 A100 GPU-hours and 20 attempted workflow evaluations per benchmark task. Folded structures and model scores were cached and reused across evaluations.

Prospective design workflow. Claude Science received a budget of 1,000 A100 GPU-hours per target, matching MolRSI. The agent determined how to schedule jobs within this budget.

Task prompts and substitutions.

Ranking workflow search. The Codex prompt for the pMHC task is reproduced below, with machine-specific paths anonymized. Path prefixes are represented by <BASELINE_ROOT>; the remaining instructions are unchanged. Claude Science, Biomni and STELLA received the same task instructions through their native interfaces. The 14 miniprotein-binder ranking tasks used the same prompt with the candidate collections, the leave-one-target-out partition of Table S9 and AUPRC as the selection metric substituted for those tasks.

Rank designed miniprotein binders against peptide-MHC class I complexes: assign a scalar score to each target–binder complex, higher for candidates that were selected in the screen.

Three properties of this data decide what a result here means. Positives are scarce: 18 across the two search collections, so a handful of candidates moves the metric and a difference of a few points of AUROC is not a reliable ordering of two workflows. The two search collections present different gp100 peptides on the same HLA-A2 scaffold and differ only in the peptide chain, while the test collection presents an unrelated peptide, so a workflow fitted to gp100-specific features will not transfer. The negatives are hard by construction: every candidate in every collection was a design that a generative pipeline already ranked highly enough to be worth ordering, so separation here will not reproduce on a designed-versus-random task.

Appendix S3 MolRSI for antibiotic discovery

S3.1 Datasets and benchmark evaluation

Dataset roles. We used 25 source tasks to accumulate experience for antibiotic workflow development and six antibacterial target tasks to evaluate its transfer. The source tasks comprised 22 absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and toxicity (ADMET) tasks from the Therapeutics Data Commons (TDC) [? ] and three cytotoxicity tasks for HepG2, HSkMC and IMR-90 cells. The antibacterial targets were activity prediction for Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. The cytotoxicity and antibacterial data were obtained from our previous study [? ]. Experience accumulated on the source tasks was used to initialize searches on the antibacterial targets; outcomes from the six target tasks were excluded from this initial memory. Table S3 lists the source tasks and their evaluation metrics.

Dataset sizes and class distributions. The six antibacterial datasets contained between 38,650 and 39,390 labelled entries each (Table S4). Positive labels were rare, ranging from 109 for P. aeruginosa to 1,321 for N. gonorrhoeae. Their prevalence varied more than tenfold across species, from 0.28% to 3.42%; negative labels accounted for the remaining 96.58–99.72%. AUPRC was used to evaluate the retrieval of these rare positives. Dataset sizes count labelled entries rather than unique molecular structures. Repeated SMILES entries were retained in the benchmark files, and their numbers are reported alongside the numbers of unique SMILES strings.

Dataset Size Positive Negative Positive (%) Unique SMILES Repeated entries
S. aureus 39,390 470 38,920 1.19 39,266 124
P. aeruginosa 39,267 109 39,158 0.28 39,266 1
A. baumannii 39,267 221 39,046 0.56 39,266 1
E. coli 39,267 222 39,045 0.57 39,266 1
K. pneumoniae 39,267 185 39,082 0.47 39,266 1
N. gonorrhoeae 38,650 1,321 37,329 3.42 38,622 28

Similarity-based data partitions. The 22 TDC tasks used the official benchmark partitions and task-specific evaluation metrics. For each of the six antibacterial and three cytotoxicity tasks, we generated five fixed partitions using random seeds 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. Molecules were represented by 2,048-bit Morgan fingerprints with radius 2 and grouped by greedy leader clustering at a Tanimoto threshold of 0.40 (greedy_leader_tanimoto). Clusters were assigned to training, validation and test sets with stratification by the binary label and target proportions of 8:1:1. All methods used the same partitions for a given task. Table S5 reports the actual sizes and positive counts for all 45 dataset–seed combinations; negative counts are obtained by subtracting positives from the corresponding split size. Within each seed, the training, validation and test sets had no overlapping dataset identifiers or exact SMILES strings.

The five seeds repartitioned the same dataset, with partially overlapping training and test sets across seeds. They therefore provided repeated evaluations on different partitions of the same data. Positive counts could vary between partitions despite label stratification. For example, S. aureus test sets contained 72–82 positives, and E. coli validation sets contained 22–50 positives. These counts are reported separately for each seed so that the class distributions underlying the validation and test scores are explicit.

Compound overlap across tasks. Compound identity across datasets was assessed by exact matching of the supplied SMILES strings. The nine antibacterial and cytotoxicity tasks contained 39,274 distinct SMILES strings in total, of which 38,583 (98.2%) were present in all nine tasks. The three cytotoxicity datasets contained the same 39,224 unique SMILES strings; 39,219 were also present in each of the P. aeruginosa, A. baumannii, E. coli and K. pneumoniae datasets. Source and target tasks thus differed in biological endpoints while drawing largely on the same compound library. These counts refer to exact SMILES strings, without additional structure standardization for the overlap analysis.

Precomputed molecular features. Each split included 2,048-bit Morgan fingerprints [? ] and 210 RDKit descriptors [? ]. Missing descriptor values were replaced by the median for that descriptor in the training set. Descriptors were standardized using means and standard deviations estimated from the training set, and the same transformation was applied to the validation and test sets. Raw and standardized descriptors were provided in the same row order as the corresponding input data.

Workflow selection and statistical reporting. Each antibacterial target involved a single workflow search. Every candidate was fitted and evaluated on all five fixed splits, and mean validation AUPRC guided search and selected the final workflow. Held-out test outcomes were not supplied as search feedback or used for workflow selection. Test AUPRC was summarized as the mean and sample standard deviation across the five splits. The standard deviation describes variation across the five data partitions. Systems were ranked separately within each task, with ties assigned their average rank. Mean ranks and mean AUPRC values gave all six tasks equal weight. AUROC denotes the area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve, and AUPRC denotes the area under the precision–recall curve.

Held-out S. aureus activity test set. The predictive comparison in Figure 3f used 271 compounds from the All tested compounds worksheet of Supplementary Data 2 in our previous study [? ]. The worksheet contained 241 screening candidates, 30 low-predicted-activity controls and 12 known-antibiotic-class positive controls. We retained the candidates and low-score controls and excluded the positive controls identified by the BLACTAM_OR_QUINOLONE categories. The resulting set contained 21 active and 250 inactive compounds. Both predictors were evaluated against the same binary labels (ACTIVITY). The published scores (ANTIBIOTIC_PS) gave an AUROC of 0.590 and an average precision of 0.090; average precision was used to calculate the comparator AUPRC. This predictive comparison was distinct from the campaign-level hit-rate comparison, which used 107 MolRSI-selected and 241 expert-selected compounds (Section S3.6.3).

S3.2 Evaluation of recursive self-improvement

Source experience. MolRSI developed workflows independently on each of the 25 source tasks and pooled the resulting experience in solution, refinement and execution memory. Each antibacterial target began with the same pooled source experience. Experience generated during a target search guided later iterations of that search and was not shared with the other targets.

Resource library and RSI conditions. The small-molecule resource library contained 110 reusable skills: 55 models, 48 methods and seven tools or resources. These covered molecular standardization, feature construction, predictive models, class-imbalance handling, calibration, stacking and ensembling. MolRSI with RSI and MolRSI without RSI used the same resource library, backbone model, data partitions, evaluation procedure and 20-attempt search allowance. MolRSI with RSI began with the pooled source experience; MolRSI without RSI began without experience from previous tasks. In both conditions, memory was updated during the current task to guide later iterations.

Search trajectories. At each iteration, we identified the completed workflow with the highest mean validation AUPRC obtained so far. Its test performance was calculated after workflow search to construct the trajectory in Figure 2d. Test scores were not returned to the agent as feedback and were excluded from memory updates.

Zero-search transfer. For Figure 2e, MolRSI identified the best-matching source task using task type, evaluation metric, dataset size and task-description similarity, and then selected the workflow with the validation performance on that source task. Both selections preceded evaluation on the antibacterial target. Model parameters were fitted on the target training data where required, but no alternative target-workflow configurations were searched.

Resource accounting. One workflow-search iteration comprised construction, execution and validation evaluation of a candidate under the accounting rules in Section S2.2. Zero-search transfer omitted target-workflow search but retained any required model fitting and inference. Skill construction, experience accumulation on source tasks, target search, final fitting and screening-library inference were separate computational stages.

Experience-pool-size analysis. We transferred one workflow from each source task to each of the six antibacterial targets, obtaining a matrix of 150 source–target evaluations. For each subset of 2–25 source tasks, we retrospectively selected the transfer test AUPRC available within that subset separately for each target, then averaged these six task performances. The mean curve in Figure 2f is the analytical expectation of this quantity over all equally sized source-task subsets.

To estimate the percentile bands, we generated 2,000 random permutations of the 25 source tasks using numpy.random.default_rng with seed 20260901. For pool size ZZ, the first ZZ tasks in each permutation defined a sampled pool, producing nested pools across sizes. We calculated the interquartile and 5th–95th percentile ranges of the six-target mean across these pools. The seed affected these sampled bands, not the analytical mean or the underlying source–target scores. The bands describe variation in pool composition, not independent search replicates or confidence intervals for the routing method. At size 25, only the complete pool was available.

S3.3 Case studies of experience-guided search

Experience-guided workflow reuse for A. baumannii. We examined how a workflow developed on AMES supported workflow selection for A. baumannii. Solution memory retained an equal-weight ensemble of LANTERN–RADR, MiniMol [? ], ADMETrix and MapLight GNN, together with their component configurations. MiniMol used IA3-based adaptation [? ] of the prediction head, a gated multilayer perceptron and class-balanced sampling. MapLight GNN used a Set2Set readout [? ] with three processing steps. The four components achieved AMES AUROCs of 0.8480–0.8633, and their ensemble achieved 0.8731 (Table S6). These configurations provided previously evaluated alternatives for the antibacterial task.

We transferred the components and their ensemble without changing their architectures or training settings. Model parameters were fitted on the A. baumannii training data, and target validation performance selected among the five inherited configurations before test evaluation. This selected LANTERN–RADR, which achieved a mean test AUPRC of 0.5356. The unchanged four-component ensemble achieved 0.4742, and the other individual components ranged from 0.3235 to 0.3863. Thus, the ensemble that performed best on AMES did not provide the best transfer performance. Retaining its component configurations allowed target validation to identify a more effective predictor without generating or refining a new workflow.

Search without experience from previous tasks evaluated 20 workflows on A. baumannii, comprising five initial model evaluations, six refinements and nine ensemble evaluations (Table S7). The refinements changed molecular features, prediction heads, class-imbalance handling and training procedures. For example, ADMETTBoost–XGBoost [? ] incorporated Morgan-fingerprint features, focal loss [? ] and bagging. Euclia-ML variants used gradient-boosting heads, class-balanced focal loss and feature selection. Ensemble evaluations combined configurations evaluated earlier in the search.

The highest observed test AUPRC increased from 0.3716 at step 1 to 0.4134 after the ADMETTBoost–XGBoost refinement at step 3. It reached 0.4335 after the Euclia-ML refinement at step 5. Ensembles then achieved 0.4572 at step 6 and 0.4988 at step 7. The remaining 13 evaluations explored additional predictors, training modifications and ensembles but did not exceed 0.4988. These evaluations included gated fusion of molecular descriptors, cosine warm restarts [? ], stochastic weight averaging [? ] and label smoothing. Additional ensemble configurations achieved test AUPRCs of 0.4005–0.4684, showing that further combinations of the evaluated models did not improve the best observed result in this run.

The validation-selected LANTERN–RADR configuration exceeded the best observed test AUPRC in the 20-step search by 0.0368, corresponding to a relative improvement of 7.4%. This advantage was obtained without further workflow refinement, while retaining target-task model fitting and validation-based selection. Within the RSI framework, solution memory contributed to the effective search policy by supplying previously evaluated configurations for the new task. In this case, selecting and reusing one of these configurations produced a better predictor than the 20-step search. The unchanged source ensemble did not exceed that search, emphasizing the contribution of selecting a suitable configuration from the accumulated experience.

S3.4 Virtual screening and compound selection

Training data and screening library. The prospective activity and cytotoxicity models used the same training datasets as our previous study [? ]. The activity models were trained on methicillin-susceptible S. aureus (MSSA; strain RN4220), and cytotoxicity was predicted for HepG2, HSkMC and IMR-90 cells. Both studies screened the same library of 12,076,365 compounds, comprising 11,277,225 entries from the Mcule purchasable database and 799,140 entries from the Broad Institute collection.

Selected screening models. The MolRSI workflow used separately optimized predictors for activity and cytotoxicity (Figure S2). HepG2 and IMR-90 cytotoxicity predictors combined MiniMol embeddings with Morgan fingerprints and RDKit descriptors and used residual multilayer-perceptron heads. The HSkMC predictor used MiniMol embeddings with gated multilayer-perceptron heads. Activity ranking combined two MiniMol-based variants and a LANTERN–RADR ensemble with weights of 0.55, 0.30 and 0.15, respectively. These weights combined the outputs of the three component-specific ensembles.

Filtering, ranking and diversity selection. Screening proceeded through structural novelty filtering, cytotoxicity filtering, activity ranking, Butina clustering and diverse picking (Figure S2). Structural filtering removed compounds matching PAINS or Brenk alerts [? ? ] or established antibiotic cores. It also required a maximum Tanimoto similarity below 0.40 to known antibiotics. The excluded core families were β\beta-lactams, quinolones, oxazolidinones, nitrofurans and sulfonamides. Cytotoxicity filtering required predicted scores of ≤0.40\leq 0.40 for each of HepG2, HSkMC and IMR-90. The retained compounds were ranked by the weighted antibacterial-activity ensemble described above. Butina clustering [? ] grouped structurally similar candidates, and diverse picking selected compounds across clusters to retain chemical diversity. We selected and experimentally tested 107 compounds; the final selection included documented exceptions to the nominal cytotoxicity criterion.

S3.5 Comparison with the previous expert-driven workflow

Workflow differences. The workflows differed in their predictive models, filter order and thresholds, and compound-selection procedures (Figure S2). The expert-driven workflow applied activity prediction before cytotoxicity and structural filtering. MolRSI applied structural filtering before cytotoxicity prediction and activity ranking. Training data and library composition are specified in Section S3.4.

Expert-developed predictors and filtering. The previous study used separate 20-member Chemprop ensembles [? ] with RDKit descriptors for S. aureus activity and for each of the three cytotoxicity tasks [? ]. Activity-score thresholds of >0.4>0.4 for Mcule and >0.2>0.2 for the Broad Institute collection retained 10,310 compounds. Requiring all three cytotoxicity scores to be <0.2<0.2 reduced this set to 3,646. PAINS/Brenk filtering retained 2,209 compounds, and similarity and antibiotic-core filtering retained 1,261. The similarity filter used a maximum Tanimoto similarity below 0.5 to training actives, and the excluded core families were β\beta-lactams and quinolones.

Candidate selection. In the expert-driven workflow, Monte Carlo tree search identified substructures supporting antibacterial predictions and informed selection of compounds with or without such rationales. Compounds were sourced according to availability and purity greater than 90%, and 241 filtered candidates were tested. The MolRSI workflow instead ranked candidates with its weighted activity ensemble and selected structurally diverse compounds across Butina clusters, leading to 107 selected and tested compounds. The substructure search in the previous study served molecular interpretation and candidate selection; it was a different application of tree search from the workflow-development search performed by MolRSI.

Comparison endpoints. Predictive discrimination was evaluated against shared labels, whereas experimental hit proportions were calculated within each campaign’s selected candidates. These analyses assess prediction and complete-workflow yield, respectively (Sections S3.1 and S3.6.3).

S3.6 Experimental validation

S3.6.1 Antibacterial activity assays

Bacterial strains and culture. S. aureus RN4220 (MSSA) was obtained from DSMZ (DSM 26309) and S. aureus FPR3757/USA300 (MRSA) from ATCC (BAA-1556). Strains were authenticated by the suppliers by next-generation or Sanger sequencing. Single colonies were picked from LB agar (1.5% Difco agar; BD 244520) and grown aerobically in liquid LB (BD 244620; 2–3 mL working volume in 14 mL Falcon tubes) at 37∘​C37\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C} with shaking at 300 rpm, without antibiotic selection.

Compounds. Compounds were purchased from ChemBridge (C3; ID 7359936) and Vitas-M Laboratories (C32; STL235206) and dissolved in DMSO (MilliporeSigma D5879) at 12.8​mg​mL−112.8\,\mathrm{mg\,mL^{-1}}.

Inoculum. A suspension of approximately 105​CFU​mL−110^{5}\,\mathrm{CFU\,mL^{-1}} was prepared either by a 1:10,000 dilution of an overnight culture picked from a single colony or by a 1:500 dilution of an OD600\mathrm{OD}_{600} 0.08 suspension in fresh LB.

MSSA screen and dose–response plates. Compounds were screened against MSSA at a single dose of 128​μ​g​mL−1128\,\mu\mathrm{g\,mL^{-1}} with a PrestoBlue readout. Compounds that inhibited growth were advanced to an eight-point two-fold dose–response series (128 to 1​μ​g​mL−11\,\mu\mathrm{g\,mL^{-1}}) in duplicate 384-well plates. Compound was dispensed from DMSO stock by acoustic dispensing (Echo; maximum DMSO 1.0%) before addition of inoculated LB to a final volume of 64​μ​L64\,\mu\mathrm{L}. Each plate carried sterility (medium only), untreated growth, Triton X-100 kill and DMSO vehicle (1.000% to 0.008%) controls.

MRSA dose–response plate. The MRSA MIC for C32 was determined in a 96-well plate with a nine-point two-fold series (128 to 0.5​μ​g​mL−10.5\,\mu\mathrm{g\,mL^{-1}}) in three replicate rows, a DMSO vehicle series, a Triton X-100 dilution series, untreated growth wells and medium-only outer wells.

Incubation and readout. Plates were covered with a lid (not sealed) and incubated for 18–24 h at 37∘​C37\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C} with 5% CO2\mathrm{CO}_{2}. OD600\mathrm{OD}_{600} was read on a SpectraMax M3 multi-mode microplate reader (Molecular Devices). MIC was the lowest concentration giving ≥90%\geq 90\% growth inhibition relative to the untreated growth control.

S3.6.2 Cytotoxicity assays

Mammalian cell culture. HepG2, HSkMC and IMR-90 cells were obtained from ATCC and maintained at 37∘​C37\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C} and 5% CO2\mathrm{CO}_{2} in humidified incubators. Cells were passaged fewer than 5–10 times before use. All lines were authenticated by ATCC using short tandem repeat profiling. Culture media are listed in Table S8.

Cell line ATCC no. Culture medium
HepG2 HB-8065 DMEM, high glucose (Corning 10-013-CV) + 10% FBS (Thermo Fisher 16140071) + 1% penicillin–streptomycin (Thermo Fisher 15070063)
HSkMC PCS-950-010 Mesenchymal Stem Cell Basal Medium for Adipose, Umbilical and Bone Marrow-derived MSCs (ATCC PCS-500-030) + Primary Skeletal Muscle Growth Kit (ATCC PCS-950-040) + 1% penicillin–streptomycin
IMR-90 CCL-186 Eagle’s Minimum Essential Medium (EMEM; ATCC 30-2003) + 10% FBS + 1% penicillin–streptomycin

Dosing and controls. Cells were plated at 55–10×10310\times 10^{3} cells per well in 96-well clear flat-bottom black tissue-culture-treated plates (Corning 3603), 100​μ​L100\,\mu\mathrm{L} per well, and dosed 24 h later. For dosing, column 2 was brought to 198​μ​L198\,\mu\mathrm{L} with medium and 2​μ​L2\,\mu\mathrm{L} of 12.8​mg​mL−112.8\,\mathrm{mg\,mL^{-1}} DMSO stock was added (128​μ​g​mL−1128\,\mu\mathrm{g\,mL^{-1}}, 1% DMSO). One hundred microlitres were then carried across nine columns by two-fold serial transfer and the final 100​μ​L100\,\mu\mathrm{L} was discarded, so that DMSO fell from 1% to 0.004% in step with compound. Untreated wells (n=4n=4) defined 100% viability. A matched DMSO series was run in separate rows. Triton X-100 (0.1% final) lysis wells defined the assay floor and were added 30–60 min before reading. Media-only wells with dye served as background.

Viability readout and analysis. PrestoBlue HS Cell Viability Reagent (Invitrogen P50200) was added at 10% of the well volume (10​μ​L10\,\mu\mathrm{L} per 100​μ​L100\,\mu\mathrm{L}) and plates were incubated for 4 h at 37∘​C37\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}. Fluorescence (excitation/emission, 550/590 nm) was read on a SpectraMax M3 multi-mode microplate reader (Molecular Devices) from the top and bottom. Viability was calculated as (well−background)/(untreated−background)×100(\text{well}-\text{background})/(\text{untreated}-\text{background})\times 100. CC50\mathrm{CC}_{50} was calculated by log2\log_{2} interpolation across the 50% crossing, and the two bracketing concentrations are reported alongside it. HepG2 values were obtained in separate earlier plates with the same PrestoBlue readout.

S3.6.3 Predictive performance and experimental hit rates

Predictive performance was evaluated as described in Section S3.1. Experimental hit rates used the 107 MolRSI-selected compounds and the 241 expert-selected candidates as their denominators. Based on the recorded endpoints, the campaigns yielded 17/107 (15.9%) and 21/241 (8.7%) hits, respectively. A hit was defined by an MSSA MIC of ≤32​μ​g​mL−1\leq 32\,\mu\mathrm{g\,mL^{-1}}, distinct from the binary labels used for predictive evaluation. The comparator denominator excluded low-predicted-activity and known-antibiotic-class controls. Hit proportions were reported with 95% Wilson binomial confidence intervals [? ]; no between-group hypothesis tests were reported. The numerical MIC threshold was aligned across studies, without assuming identical experimental protocols.

Appendix S4 MolRSI for peptide–MHC binder design

S4.1 Datasets and benchmark evaluation

The protein study comprised 14 independent miniprotein-binder design tasks, each with one held-out target, followed by one pMHC binder-design task using both gp100 datasets for workflow search and MART-1 for testing. The resulting pipeline was also used for prospective binder generation (Section 4.3). Protein experiments used no small-molecule memory records.

Miniprotein-binder experience tasks. The fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 (FGFR2), insulin receptor (InsulinR), platelet-derived growth factor receptor (PDGFR), transforming growth factor-β\beta (TGFβ\beta), interleukin-7 receptor-α\alpha (IL-7Rα\alpha), VirB8-like protein from Rickettsia typhi (VirB8), epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), tropomyosin receptor kinase A (TrkA), influenza A H3 haemagglutinin (H3), and angiopoietin-1 receptor (TIE2) datasets were obtained from Cao et al. [? ]. The SARS-CoV-2 spike receptor-binding domain (SARS-CoV-2 RBD) dataset was obtained from Cao et al. [? ]. The anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK), leukocyte tyrosine kinase (LTK), and interleukin-2 receptor-α\alpha (IL-2Rα\alpha) datasets were obtained from Bennett et al. [? ]. The source datasets provide binary binding labels at 4,000 and 400 nM. We used the source-provided 4,000-nM label as the benchmark outcome. Across the 14 retained targets, the source collections contained 901,670 designs. To construct a computationally tractable benchmark while preserving all positive examples, we retained all 1,565 positive designs and sampled up to ten negative designs per positive within each target. The resulting benchmark contained 17,215 designs: 1,565 positives and 15,650 sampled negatives (Table S9).

Each of the 14 targets defined a distinct design task under a leave-one-target-out partition. Workflow search used the other 13 targets, with AUPRC guiding selection. The selected workflow was frozen and then evaluated on the held-out target. Held-out-target labels and performance were excluded from search and workflow selection. The tasks ran independently without cross-task memory. Records of the evaluated workflows, modifications and execution outcomes were subsequently pooled into the protein-domain memory 𝒵mini\mathcal{Z}_{\mathrm{mini}} used for the pMHC task. This source memory contained no pMHC or prospective-design outcomes.

pMHC benchmark data. The single pMHC task used datasets generated by the experimental screening procedure described by Liu et al. [? ]. For all three candidate collections, the binary outcome indicated whether a candidate was selected in the fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) experiment. Selected candidates were labelled positive and unselected candidates negative.

The task included HLA-A2 complexes presenting the gp100-derived peptides YLEPGPVTA and IMDQVPFSV, and HLA-A*02:01 complexes presenting MART-1 (A2L; ELAGIGILTV). The source structures for the two gp100 complexes were PDB 5EU3 and 6VM9, respectively. All three candidate collections belonged to one pMHC benchmark task. Both gp100 collections were used directly for workflow search, whereas MART-1 comprised the held-out test set. AUROC on the gp100 collections guided workflow selection. The selected workflow was frozen before evaluation on MART-1, whose labels and performance were excluded from workflow search, selection and memory updates. Table S10 gives the dataset roles, sizes and class counts. Figure 4c reports test enrichment for MART-1.

Metric calculation and aggregation. EF was calculated as defined in Equation 2. Macro EF and AUPRC gave equal weight to each held-out target for the miniprotein-binder benchmark.

S4.2 Fixed expert-defined ranking objectives

Fixed objectives from established expert-defined design pipelines. BoltzGen [? ], BindCraft [? ], and PXDesign [? ] are complete binder design pipelines. For the retrospective ranking benchmarks, we isolated a fixed loss or ranking criterion used internally by each pipeline and evaluated it retrospectively on the same target–binder sequence pairs. Thus, these references compare the criteria used to prioritize designs.

BoltzGen used its worst-rank quality criterion on Boltz-2 [? ] predictions. If ri​jr_{ij} is the within-target percentile rank of candidate ii under metric jj, with smaller ranks better, the reported higher-is-better score was qi=−maxj⁡ri​jq_{i}=-\max_{j}r_{ij}. The primary three-metric reference used equal rank weights for design_iiptm (which restricts the design side of the pTM calculation to residues within 8​Å8\,\text{\AA} of the target), design_ptm, and the negative minimum design-to-target PAE. This is the confidence-only form of the BoltzGen criterion. The complete pipeline additionally ranks PLIP [? ] hydrogen bonds, PLIP salt bridges, and Δ\DeltaSASA. We evaluated both the three-confidence-score and six-score forms and report the former as the stronger, and therefore more conservative, fixed comparator.

For BindCraft, we reproduced the default eight-term default_4stage_multimer design loss,

LBindCraft=0.1​ℓpLDDT+0.4​ℓPAE+0.1​ℓiPAE+1.0​ℓcontact+1.0​ℓinterface​contact+0.3​ℓRg+0.05​ℓipTM−0.3​ℓhelix,\begin{split}L_{\mathrm{BindCraft}}={}&0.1\,\ell_{\mathrm{pLDDT}}+0.4\,\ell_{\mathrm{PAE}}+0.1\,\ell_{\mathrm{iPAE}}+1.0\,\ell_{\mathrm{contact}}+1.0\,\ell_{\mathrm{interface\ contact}}\\ &+0.3\,\ell_{\mathrm{Rg}}+0.05\,\ell_{\mathrm{ipTM}}-0.3\,\ell_{\mathrm{helix}},\end{split}

with the termini-distance loss disabled as in the default configuration. Terms were evaluated from AlphaFold2-Multimer-v3 [? ] predictions with target-chain MSAs. The benchmark score was −LBindCraft-L_{\mathrm{BindCraft}}, so that larger values were better.

For PXDesign, we reproduced the seven-term PXDesign-h hallucination loss on Protenix-Mini [? ] predictions,

LPXDesign=0.15​ℓpLDDT+0.4​ℓPAE+0.1​ℓiPAE+1.0​ℓcontact+1.0​ℓinterface​contact−0.3​ℓhelix+0.3​ℓRg,\begin{split}L_{\mathrm{PXDesign}}={}&0.15\,\ell_{\mathrm{pLDDT}}+0.4\,\ell_{\mathrm{PAE}}+0.1\,\ell_{\mathrm{iPAE}}+1.0\,\ell_{\mathrm{contact}}+1.0\,\ell_{\mathrm{interface\ contact}}\\ &-0.3\,\ell_{\mathrm{helix}}+0.3\,\ell_{\mathrm{Rg}},\end{split}

and again used its negative as the higher-is-better benchmark score.

Because the retrospective candidate collection did not contain pipeline-native starting backbones, this comparison did not reproduce generator-specific initial-guess or design-to-refold RMSD filters, iterative sequence optimization, or final diversity selection. It should therefore be interpreted as a comparison of fixed internal objectives from the three design pipelines rather than an end-to-end comparison of the pipelines themselves.

S4.3 Ranking benchmark results

Miniprotein-binder benchmark. Figure S3 compares the five agent workflows and the three fixed expert-defined objectives using macro EF at the 1%, 2%, 5% and 10% cutoffs and macro AUPRC. Each macro metric gives the 14 targets equal weight. MolRSI achieved macro EF values of 8.01 at 1% and 7.29 at 2%, with Biomni next at 1% (7.62) and Claude Science next at 2% (6.71). At 5%, Claude Science had a macro EF of 5.56, compared with 5.55 for MolRSI. At 10%, MolRSI had the highest macro EF (4.11). MolRSI also achieved the highest macro AUPRC (0.4305), followed by Claude Science (0.4237). Among the eight methods, MolRSI ranked first by AUPRC on six targets, with mean target-level rank 2.43, compared with 2.79 for Claude Science. Table S11 summarizes all target-level EF and AUPRC performance.

pMHC test results. Figure S4 compares test AUPRC for the five agent workflows and the three fixed expert-defined objectives on MART-1. Agent workflows were selected using the gp100 search data and frozen before test evaluation. MolRSI achieved the highest AUPRC on MART-1 (0.0172), compared with positive-fraction references of 0.0070 and the second highest AUPRC values of 0.0122 for BindCraft.

Table S12 reports all four EF cutoffs and AUPRC. MolRSI achieved the highest EF across all four cutoffs among agent baselines on MART-1. Against the three fixed expert-defined objectives, MolRSI achieved higher AUPRC and the highest EF in three of the four EF cutoffs. These results show broadly improved ranking performance across both precision–recall and enrichment metrics.

Effect of source task memory. The pMHC searches with and without miniprotein-binder memory used the same resource library, candidate data, search controller, development objective and evaluation procedure, with a 300 A100 GPU-hour budget and allowance of 20 attempted workflow evaluations. Both conditions used the complete gp100 collections for search and retained memory updates during the current search. The selected workflows were frozen before test evaluation.

Source-task memory increased MART-1 AUPRC from 0.0125 to 0.0172, a relative improvement of approximately 37% (Figure S4). It increased EF from 0.00 to 3.65 at the 1% cutoff and from 0.00 to 5.55 at the 2% cutoff. At the 5% and 10% cutoffs, EF increased from 1.48 to 2.21 and from 1.48 to 2.22, respectively (Table S13).

Selected pMHC ranking workflow. MolRSI selected a workflow using ESMFold2-Fast [? ] and an equal-weight sum of eight terms: binder_target_contact, helix_score, binder_ptm, binder_target_iptm, ptm_energy, ipsae_min, monomer_plddt and monomer_helix. Each term was oriented so that a larger value represented a more favorable predicted property before aggregation.

S4.4 Binder generation and candidate selection

Design targets. Each prospective design task was specified by an HLA allele, an on-target and off-target peptide pair, source structures for sequence and hotspot provenance, chain assignments, a binder-length range, and exposed peptide hotspots (Table S14). Within each target pair, the HLA heavy-chain and β2\beta_{2}-microglobulin sequences were held fixed and only the peptide sequence was changed. The source PDB coordinates were not supplied as design inputs. They were used only to establish the target-chain sequences and select peptide hotspots. Following previous work [? ], hotspots were selected from solvent-exposed, upward-facing peptide residues with relative solvent-accessible surface area (relSASA) of at least 20% in the binder-free pMHC complex. Individual binder lengths were sampled within the target-specific allowed range.

Generation workflow search configuration. The available generation methods were RFDiffusion3 [? ], Proteina-Complexa [? ], PXDesign [? ], BoltzGen [? ], and the MOSAIC [? ] simplex accelerated proximal gradient method (APGM). The methods differed at the generation stage and entered the same inverse-folding and ranking procedure.

The target-specific searches ran in parallel without exchanging evaluations or search records. Each search was allocated 30 attempted rounds and 1,000 A100 GPU-hours. At each node, MolRSI evaluated a generator configuration by generating 20 backbones and applying SolubleMPNN [? ] to generate eight sequences for each retained backbone, followed by the remaining scoring steps. Cysteine was excluded from the inverse-folding sequence alphabet in all workflows. The ranking score among the top-ranked 5% of designs defined the configuration’s development reward.

After the 30-round search for each target, the three highest-scoring workflows were each used to generate 8,000 additional designs. The final candidate pool comprised all designs from the search and expansion stages and was then subjected to deduplication, filtering, and ranking. We denote the exported fields on_target_ranking_score and off_target_ranking_score by sons_{\mathrm{on}} and soffs_{\mathrm{off}}, respectively. For final MolRSI selection, designs were retained when on_ipsae_min≥0.50\texttt{on\_ipsae\_min}\geq 0.50, monomer_plddt≥0.80\texttt{monomer\_plddt}\geq 0.80, at least 15 HLA contacts (hla_res≥15\texttt{hla\_res}\geq 15), and s8_on−s8_off>0\texttt{s8\_on}-\texttt{s8\_off}>0. Passing designs were ranked by s8_on.

S4.5 Comparison with reference design workflows

Prospective agent comparison. We selected Claude Science as the prospective baseline because it achieved the highest performance on the miniprotein-binder benchmark and had previously demonstrated autonomous design of experimentally validated protein binders [? ]. The completed comparison comprised independent target-specific campaigns for MART-1 and SARS-CoV-1. The target and peptide-swapped off-target specifications, binder-length range, design objectives and total computational budget were held fixed, while each system retained its native generation, refinement and ranking procedure. Both systems received 1,000 A100 GPU-hours per target. The 30-round allowance applied to MolRSI’s workflow search; Claude Science instead controlled job scheduling within the shared GPU-hour budget.

Claude Science run configuration for prospective binder design. We initialized one independent Claude Science session per target, using Claude Opus 5 and an adaptation of Anthropic’s multi-target binder-design protocol [? ]. The prompt source is provided in Section S2.3; this section summarizes the study-specific adaptations and run configuration.

We adapted the instructions to peptide-specific pMHC design and the available computing platform. Inputs comprised HLA heavy-chain and β2\beta_{2}-microglobulin sequences and MSAs, on- and off-target peptide sequences, an 80–120-residue binder range, epitope hints and novelty references. Every scoring prediction was required to include the HLA heavy chain, β2\beta_{2}-microglobulin, peptide and binder. Epitope positions were hints, not a mandatory hotspot-contact filter.

The campaign was given a computational budget of 1,000 A100 GPU-hours per target, with job state recorded in files on a shared volume. SolubleMPNN [? ] and SolubleCaliby [? ] were named for designs selected for the final computational output, with their base variants permitted during backbone search. The specified pipeline placed checks for sequence and structural novelty, liabilities, monomer foldability, structural plausibility and redundancy before any complex prediction.

The instructions required retained candidates to be scored against the on- and off-target complexes using ESMFold2-Fast, ESMFold2-Full [? ] and Protenix v2 [? ]. For each scoring model, the fixed criterion combined minimum ipSAE [? ], design-to-prediction scDockQ [? ] and the on-target-minus-off-target minimum-ipSAE difference. Scores were standardized within the candidate cohort and combined with relative weights of 4:1:44{:}1{:}4. The minimum scDockQ across the scoring models used also entered the ranking key at a prespecified pose threshold of 0.23, ordering designs that met it above those that did not. At least two rounds of partial diffusion, prediction followed by redesign, or sequence resampling were required. The requested output was a ranked set of 500 designs per target, excluding exact and near duplicates and limiting representation from individual design lineages and structural clusters. At least three structure generators had to be represented, with no more than 50% of designs from one generator or two-thirds from one sequence-design method.

The authors specified the target inputs, scoring criterion, output format, diversity limits and computational budget. Claude Science chose the generation strategy and parameters, sampling allocation, use of epitope hints, monomer and structural-plausibility thresholds, parent selection and refinement operations. The monomer and structural-plausibility thresholds were fixed after selection. The comparison therefore used its native binder-design protocol with pMHC- and platform-specific adaptations.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
